> **RU:** Git-политика GCW — trunk-based с короткими feature-ветками, PR обязателен для merge в main.
> **RU:** Коммиты на английском (Conventional Commits); release/hotfix через отдельные ветки; force-push запрещён.

# Git Workflow Policy

## Applies to / Применяется

All agents operating on a Git-tracked GCW repository **must** follow this
workflow when producing non-trivial changes; trivial changes (typo fixes,
single-line docs polish) may be committed directly to the working branch,
but the same review policy still applies before merge.

**Full branching/release/hotfix procedure:** load skill `git-workflow-detailed`.

---

## Core rule

**No change lands in `main` without a reviewed pull request from a feature branch.**

`main` is the protected, always-green baseline. The only commits on `main` are:

- **Baseline imports** (the initial commit when a new repository is set up).
- **Fast-forward merges** of approved PRs from feature branches.
- **Hotfix merges** for production-grade emergencies, which are themselves
  required to come from a `hotfix/*` branch with at least one review.
- **Release merges** from `release/*` branches (merge commit, preserves history).

Branch types: `feat/...`, `fix/...`, `docs/...`, `refactor/...`, `chore/...`,
`release/...`, `hotfix/...`, `experiment/...` (never merged); naming
`<type>/<ticket-id-or-slug>` (kebab-case). Full branching model and Mermaid
diagrams: skill `git-workflow-detailed`.

---

## Commit message format — Conventional Commits

**Always English**, regardless of conversation language (per
`communication-language.instructions.md`).

```text
[type]([scope]): [description]           # mandatory
                                         # blank line
[optional body — 1-3 short paragraphs]    # 72-char wrap
                                         # blank line
[optional footer — issue/PR refs, BREAKING CHANGE notes]
```

### Allowed `type` values

| Type | When |
| --- | --- |
| `feat` | A new user-visible feature / capability |
| `fix` | A bug fix |
| `docs` | Documentation only |
| `style` | Whitespace / formatting (no logic change) |
| `refactor` | Code change with no behavior change |
| `perf` | Performance improvement |
| `test` | Adding or fixing tests |
| `build` | Build / CI / dependency changes |
| `chore` | Tooling / scripts / non-source housekeeping |
| `revert` | Reverts a previous commit (use `git revert`) |
| `hotfix` | Emergency production fix (merged fast-forward) |
| `release` | Release cut / version bump (on release branches) |

### Examples

```text
feat(0.5): add minimax-m3 ollama fallback to high-stakes tiers
hotfix(v1.4.3): fix connection pool leak in production
```

### Breaking changes

Add `BREAKING CHANGE:` in the footer (or `!` after the type/scope):
`feat(agents)!: require handoffs: on every user-invocable senior`.
During 0.x.x: breaking changes bump MINOR, not MAJOR, but still use
the `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer for visibility.

---

## Semantic commit grouping

> **RU:** Семантическая группировка коммитов — один логический темат = один коммит.
> **RU:** Коммиты не бампают версию; только release-процесс это делает. Changelog формируется из раздела `[Unreleased]`.

Group changes by **logical theme**, not by session or by file; each
group gets its own commit, and `git bisect` can isolate a regression
to a single theme. Commits add bullets to `## [Unreleased]` in
`CHANGELOG.md`; version bumps happen only at release time (see
"Versioning cadence" below).

### Core rule

- **One commit = one theme** (see the When-to-apply table for
  scenarios); a session with 3 themes (feature + bugfix + docs)
  becomes 3 commits, not one blob.
- **Commits do not bump versions.** Releases do — the Git Workflow
  Specialist decides when `[Unreleased]` is "enough" and applies one
  SemVer bump at release time (see "Versioning cadence" below).
- **Commit message follows Conventional Commits** (`type(scope): description`),
  as defined above — no version suffix; the CHANGELOG section carries
  the version at release time.

### When to apply

| Scenario | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Multi-session work that touched the same files across sessions | Reconstruct intermediate file states per commit (`git add -p` or stash + reapply) |
| Single session with multiple logical themes (e.g. bugfix + feature + docs) | Split into N commits, one per theme; add one bullet each to `[Unreleased]` |
| Single session with one theme | One commit, no split needed |
| Theme spans multiple files that must ship together (e.g. schema migration + consumers) | One commit — the theme is "schema migration", not "per-file" |

### Example

AgentsNode 2026-07-19: 3 sessions dumped into 1 blob (`feat: agentsnode
0.9.2` with secrets refactor + 3 chart bugs + 4 review findings in the
body) — reader cannot tell which lines belong to which theme, changelog
opaque, bisect broken. The same work as 3 semantic commits (version
assigned at release time):

```text
feat(secrets): refactor to SOPS manifest
fix(helm): resolve 3 chart bugs — restore job, stdin/tty, gateway down-file
fix(review): apply 4 code-review findings
```

### Conflict resolution

- Composes with the core rule ("No change lands in `main` without a
  reviewed pull request") — splitting happens **inside** the feature
  branch before the PR; the PR still requires review.
- If a theme spans multiple files that must ship together (schema
  migration + consumers), they stay in **one commit** — the theme is
  "schema migration", not "per-file"; splitting atomic units breaks
  bisect and review.
- Prefer `git add -p` for surgical staging; use stash + reapply only
  when the sessions' changes genuinely interleave in the same hunks.

`## [Unreleased]` in `CHANGELOG.md`; the Git Workflow Specialist decides
when `[Unreleased]` is "enough" and cuts a release — one SemVer bump,
tagging, GitHub release. Other seniors merge PRs; they do not bump versions.

### Release criteria

The Git Workflow Specialist evaluates ALL criteria together. No single
criterion forces a release. Half-finished releases are unacceptable.

| # | Criterion | Type | Deciding? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Logical group complete (feature + bugfixes fully done) | Readiness | YES |
| 2 | Cap reached (≥10 patch-level changes in [Unreleased]) | Signal | NO — attracts attention, does not force |
| 3 | Owner requests release | Request | YES |
| 4 | Breaking change ready for release | Readiness | YES |
| 5 | 14-day floor (no [Unreleased] untouched >14 days without deferral note) | Signal | NO |
| 6 | CI green at cut time | Gate | YES (non-negotiable, but not a trigger) |

mandatory, but not a trigger: 10 patches with an unfinished feature →
wait; 3 patches with a done feature and an owner request → release.

|---|---|---|
| `feat:` (new feature) | MINOR | MINOR |
| `fix:` / `refactor:` / `docs:` / `test:` / `chore:` | PATCH | PATCH |
| `feat!:` (breaking) | MINOR + `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer | MAJOR |

add bullets there, and the Specialist decides when to promote it to a
dated release section with a version bump. The 13-step release
process (skill `git-workflow-detailed`) is the ONLY path to a version
bump — there are no per-commit version bumps.

### Git Workflow Specialist is sole release owner

Only `@GCW: Git Workflow Specialist` (or the owner directly) decides
when to cut a release and applies the version bump; other agents
delegate per the `scope-discipline.instructions.md` hard routing rule.

### Transition to 1.0

`1.0.0` is a public API stability commitment, not a version counter
threshold. The owner evaluates before declaring 1.0:

- Public API documented and frozen — no pending breaking changes
- At least one external adopter has run a release cycle without issues
- Test coverage at agreed threshold (QA Engineer signs off)
- CHANGELOG cleaned; migration guide `0.x → 1.0` written (Tech Writer)
- Owner explicitly declares "1.0 ready" — never automatic

Post-1.0, breaking changes → MAJOR (not minor); the `0.x` "breaking = minor +
`BREAKING CHANGE:` footer" rule retires at 1.0.

---

## Merged-file control before merge/rebase (merge-tree gate)

`mergeable = true` in a PR UI and a "clean" rebase prove the text merges —
they say NOTHING about whether the merged result is correct. Before every
merge or rebase that touches files formed by bullet-accumulation
(`CHANGELOG.md` first of all), run `git merge-tree --write-tree HEAD
<branch>` (or `HEAD` vs `origin/main` before a rebase) and check the
merged result, not just the exit code: no duplicated headers, no lost
bullets, preamble intact, new entries landing in `[Unreleased]` — never
inside a closed release section. The trap this closes: two branches each
append "under `[Unreleased]`" at the same anchor, the merged file silently
interleaves foreign bullets into the previous release's section or drops
them; git reports zero conflicts. Full procedure: skill
`git-workflow-detailed` § "Merged-file control (merge-tree gate)".

---

## Subagent invocation discipline

When a senior delegates to a subagent that returns synthesis, **the
senior commits** — not the subagent. If a subagent reports diff
suggestions, the senior reviews, applies, runs local checks, then
commits. This prevents "phantom commits" where a chain of delegations
leaves the working tree inconsistent.

---

## Report and description language (Git Workflow Specialist)

Release descriptions, PR bodies, and delegation briefs produced by the
Git Workflow Specialist follow the prose quality standard
(`response-style.instructions.md` § "Prose quality standard
(project-wide)"): plain, professional, no session-shorthand. **The owner
reads these texts** — jargon from the working session ("mechanical
shipping", "ride-along", "escape-hatch", component nicknames) must not
survive into them; every abbreviation expands on first use and every
internal codename carries a one-line gloss.

Release descriptions specifically follow skill `release-notes` (curated
prose with the summary paragraph + highlighted changes as the mandatory
minimum — never a pasted changelog dump). A PR body or a brief is a
report: state what changed and why it matters in sentences a reader
outside the session can parse on first pass.

---

## One lane in the main tree (parallel lanes via worktree)

**One working lane per tree.** Parallel work lanes NEVER share the main
working tree: two agents editing the same checkout interleave their
staging areas, stomp each other's `HEAD`, and mix commits from different
themes into one index — the semantic commit grouping above becomes
unenforceable. Parallel lanes are strictly `git worktree` lanes:

1. **Create the worktree per lane** — `git worktree add ../gcw-lane-<name>
   -b feat/<lane>`; each lane commits only in its own worktree.
2. **File-zone map before launching a wave** — before multiple lanes run
   in parallel, write down (in the wave brief) which files/dirs each lane
   may touch. Two lanes whose zones overlap either merge into one lane or
   run serially; overlapping zones plus parallel lanes equals guaranteed
   conflict on merge.
3. **Merge back one lane at a time** through the normal PR flow, in a
   fixed order recorded in the wave brief; each merge re-runs the
   merged-file control above on the CHANGELOG-carrying lanes.

This rule does not change the PR policy — every lane still merges to
`main` through a reviewed PR. It constrains WHERE parallel work happens.

---

## Issue closure discipline + instant priority filing

- **Closure = full record, not a state flip.** Closing an issue requires
  a closing comment containing: the merge SHA (or commit range) that
  resolved it, the verification verdicts with cited outputs (per
  `gcw-agent-behavior.instructions.md` §11), and the fate of the tail
  (follow-ups deferred → each one already filed, see below). An issue
  closed without this record is a silent loss: the next reader cannot
  tell what was proven or what was punted.
- **Actionable finding → issue immediately, with priority.** Any finding
  worth acting on (review tail, deferred fix, observed defect) is filed
  as an issue at the moment it is identified — with a priority label —
  not kept in prose, chat, or memory. Unfiled findings get lost;
  findings filed without priority rot in the backlog. The 2026-08-31
  backlog loss (queue preserved only because it was re-filed as an
  issue) is the evidence for this rule.
- **TEMP-WORKAROUND is a contract, not a tag.** A temporary workaround
  may ship ONLY together with its replacement condition: the tracking
  issue link (with priority) stating what replaces it and when. A
  "temporary" workaround without a replacement condition is a permanent
  workaround wearing a mask — same defect, now with documentation.

---

## Toggling this rule off (opt-out)

This is a **project-wide rule**. Two supported opt-out mechanisms:

1. **Per-file ignore (recommended)** — rename to
   `git-workflow.instructions.md.disabled`; VS Code picks up only
   `*.instructions.md`. Re-enable by removing the suffix.
2. **Per-agent scope override** — a more specific rule in an agent
   body or a scoped `*.instructions.md` with a narrower `applyTo`
   glob wins within its domain.

There is no in-file toggle: VS Code does not support instruction-level
flags — renaming is the canonical escape hatch.

---

## See also

- `communication-language.instructions.md` — language rules (English commits).
- `lint-and-validate.instructions.md` — finding → fix, not suppress; CI gates.
- `docs-sync-runtime.instructions.md` — post-slice docs sync.
- `scope-discipline.instructions.md` — routing + hand-off discipline.
- `sensitive-data.instructions.md` — secret material in commits.
- `destructive-actions.instructions.md` — destructive git ops (`push --force`, `reset --hard` on shared branches, `branch -D`, tag deletion/force-move).
- Skill `git-workflow-detailed` — full branching, versioning, release, hotfix, tagging, branch protection, CI/CD, changelog, backporting procedures.

minimum — never a pasted changelog dump). A PR body or a brief is a
report: state what changed and why it matters in sentences a reader
outside the session can parse on first pass.

---

## One lane in the main tree (parallel lanes via worktree)

**One working lane per tree.** Parallel work lanes NEVER share the main
working tree: two agents editing the same checkout interleave their
staging areas, stomp each other's `HEAD`, and mix commits from different
themes into one index — the semantic commit grouping above becomes
unenforceable. Parallel lanes are strictly `git worktree` lanes:

1. **Create the worktree per lane** — `git worktree add ../gcw-lane-<name>
   -b feat/<lane>`; each lane commits only in its own worktree.
2. **File-zone map before launching a wave** — before multiple lanes run
   in parallel, write down (in the wave brief) which files/dirs each lane
   may touch. Two lanes whose zones overlap either merge into one lane or
   run serially; overlapping zones plus parallel lanes equals guaranteed
   conflict on merge.
3. **Merge back one lane at a time** through the normal PR flow, in a
   fixed order recorded in the wave brief; each merge re-runs the
   merged-file control above on the CHANGELOG-carrying lanes.

This rule does not change the PR policy — every lane still merges to
`main` through a reviewed PR. It constrains WHERE parallel work happens.

---

## Issue closure discipline + instant priority filing

- **Closure = full record, not a state flip.** Closing an issue requires
  a closing comment containing: the merge SHA (or commit range) that
  resolved it, the verification verdicts with cited outputs (per
  `gcw-agent-behavior.instructions.md` §11), and the fate of the tail
  (follow-ups deferred → each one already filed, see below). An issue
  closed without this record is a silent loss: the next reader cannot
  tell what was proven or what was punted.
- **Actionable finding → issue immediately, with priority.** Any finding
  worth acting on (review tail, deferred fix, observed defect) is filed
  as an issue at the moment it is identified — with a priority label —
  not kept in prose, chat, or memory. Unfiled findings get lost;
  findings filed without priority rot in the backlog. The 2026-08-31
  backlog loss (queue preserved only because it was re-filed as an
  issue) is the evidence for this rule.
- **TEMP-WORKAROUND is a contract, not a tag.** A temporary workaround
  may ship ONLY together with its replacement condition: the tracking
  issue link (with priority) stating what replaces it and when. A
  "temporary" workaround without a replacement condition is a permanent
  workaround wearing a mask — same defect, now with documentation.

---

## Toggling this rule off (opt-out)

This is a **project-wide rule**. Two supported opt-out mechanisms:

1. **Per-file ignore (recommended)** — rename to
   `git-workflow.instructions.md.disabled`; VS Code picks up only
   `*.instructions.md`. Re-enable by removing the suffix.
2. **Per-agent scope override** — a more specific rule in an agent
   body or a scoped `*.instructions.md` with a narrower `applyTo`
   glob wins within its domain.

There is no in-file toggle: VS Code does not support instruction-level
flags — renaming is the canonical escape hatch.

---

- `docs-sync-runtime.instructions.md` — post-slice docs sync.
